using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n219\t\n220\t     Notes\n221\t     -----\n222\t\n223\t        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n224\t        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n225\t        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n226\t\n227\t        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n228\t        source plane. For e.g. source normal along ``z``, the normal components (``Ez`` and ``Hz``)\n229\t        can be provided but will have no effect on the results, and at least one of the tangential\n230\t        components has to be in the dataset, i.e. at least one of ``Ex``, ``Ey``, ``Hx``, and ``Hy``.\n231\t\n232\t        .. TODO add image here\n233\t\n234\t        ..\n235\t            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n236\t            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n237\t            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n238\t            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n239\t\n240\t        ..\n241\t            TODO add example for this standalone\n242\t            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n243\t            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n244\t\n245\t        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n246\t        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n247\t        provided. An empty normalizing run may be needed to accurately normalize results.\n248\t\n249\t        To create this empty simulation it is recommended that users create a simulation with no structures but just a flux\n250\t        monitor (``tidy3D.FluxMonitor``) next to the custom source, ensuring that the flux monitor is at least one grid cell\n251\t        away from the source. Moreover, for accurate normalization, users must ensure that the same grid is used to run\n252\t        the original simulation as well as the empty simulation. The total flux calculated at the flux monitor of the empty\n253\t        simulation can then be used for proper normalization of results after ``tidy3d`` simulation.\n254\t\n255\t        The coordinates of all provided fields are assumed to be relative to the source center.\n256\t        In other words, the dataset is interpreted in a local coordinate frame centered at\n257\t        :attr:`center`; when injecting/interpolating, the simulation-space coordinates are\n258\t        ``dataset_coords + center``. This means the same dataset can be translated in space by\n259\t        changing :attr:`center` without modifying dataset coordinates.\n260\t        If only the ``E`` or only the ``H`` fields are provided, the source will not be directional,\n261\t        but will inject equal power in both directions instead.\n262\t\n263\t    Example\n264\t    -------\n265\t    >>> from tidy3d import ScalarFieldDataArray, GaussianPulse\n266\t    >>> import tidy3d as td\n267\t    >>> pulse = GaussianPulse(freq0=200e12, fwidth=20e12)\n268\t    >>> x = np.linspace(-1, 1, 101)\n269\t    >>> y = np.linspace(-1, 1, 101)\n270\t    >>> z = np.array([0])\n271\t    >>> f = [2e14]\n272\t    >>> coords = dict(x=x, y=y, z=z, f=f)\n273\t    >>> scalar_field = ScalarFieldDataArray(np.ones((101, 101, 1, 1)), coords=coords)\n274\t    >>> dataset = FieldDataset(Ex=scalar_field)\n275\t    >>> custom_source = CustomFieldSource(\n276\t    ...     center=(1, 1, 1),\n277\t    ...     size=(2, 2, 0),\n278\t    ...     source_time=pulse,\n279\t    ...     field_dataset=dataset)\n280\t\n281\t    Creating an empty simulation with no structures with ``FluxMonitor`` for normalization but with the same grid as the\n282\t    original simulation.\n283\t\n284\t    Example\n285\t    -------\n286\t    >>> Flux_monitor = td.FluxMonitor(\n287\t    ...     center=(0, 0, 0),\n288\t    ...     size=(3, 3, 3),\n289\t    ...     freqs=f,\n290\t    ...     name=\"Flux\",\n291\t    ...     )\n292\t    >>> sim = td.Simulation(\n293\t    ...       center=[0,0,0],\n294\t    ...       size=(4, 4, 4),\n295\t    ...       structures=[],\n296\t    ...       sources=[custom_source],\n297\t    ...       monitors=[],\n298\t    ...       run_time = 1e-6,\n299\t    ...       shutoff=1e-6,\n300\t    ...    )\n301\t    >>> sim_empty = sim.updated_copy(monitors = [Flux_monitor],  # Illustrated\n648\t        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n649\t        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n650\t        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n651\t        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n652\t        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n653\t        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n654\t        there is radiation into the substrate.\n655\t\n656\t        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n657\t\n658\t        **Practical Advice**\n659\t\n660\t        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n661\t        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n662\t        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly. Avoid placing mode\n663\t        sources at tapers, junctions, or other locations where the cross-section is changing.\n664\t\n665\t        .. TODO improve links to other APIs functionality here.\n666\t\n667\t    Example\n668\t    -------\n669\t    >>> from tidy3d import GaussianPulse\n670\t    >>> pulse = GaussianPulse(freq0=200e12, fwidth=20e12)\n671\t    >>> mode_spec = ModeSpec(target_neff=2.)\n672\t    >>> mode_source = ModeSource(\n673\t    ...     size=(10,10,0),\n674\t    ...     source_time=pulse,\n675\t    ...     mode_spec=mode_spec,\n676\t    ...     mode_index=1,\n677\t    ...     direction='-')\n678\t\n679\t    See Also\n680\t    --------\n681\t\n682\t    :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver`:\n683\t        Interface for solving electromagnetic eigenmodes in a 2D plane with translational invariance in the third dimension.\n684\t\n685\t    **Notebooks:**\n686\t        * `Waveguide Y junction <../../notebooks/YJunction.html>`_\n687\t        * `90 degree optical hybrid <../../notebooks/90OpticalHybrid.html>`_\n688\t\n689\t    **Lectures:**\n690\t        * `Prelude to Integrated Photonics Simulation: Mode Injection <https://www.flexcompute.com/fdtd101/Lecture-4-Prelude-to-Integrated-Photonics-Simulation-Mode-Injection/>`_\n691\t    \"\"\"\n692\t\n693\t    mode_index: NonNegativeInt = Field(\n694\t        0,\n695\t        title=\"Mode Index\",\n696\t        description=\"Index into the collection of modes returned by mode solver. \"\n697\t        \" Specifies which mode to inject using this source. \"\n698\t        \"If larger than ``mode_spec.num_modes``, \"\n699\t        \"``num_modes`` in the solver will be set to ``mode_index + 1``.\",\n700\t    )\n701\t\n702\t\n703\t\"\"\" Angled Field Sources one can use. \"\"\"\n704\t\n705\t\n706\tclass AbstractAngularSpec(Tidy3dBaseModel, ABC):\n707\t    \"\"\"Abstract base for defining angular variability specifications for plane waves.\"\"\"\n708\t\n709\t\n710\tclass FixedInPlaneKSpec(AbstractAngularSpec):\n711\t    \"\"\"Plane wave is injected such that its in-plane wavevector is constant. The pole-residue method \"\n        \"can be more accurate for highly dispersive modes and uses fewer broadband terms \"\n        \"than frequency samples.\",\n    )\n\n    @model_validator(mode=\"after\")\n    def _validate_num_freqs_limit(self) -> Self:\n        \"\"\"Enforce method-specific bounds on num_freqs.\"\"\"\n        if self.broadband_method == \"chebyshev\" and self.num_freqs > 20:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='chebyshev', 'num_freqs' must be <= 20, got {self.num_freqs}.\"\n            )\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\" and self.num_freqs < 3:\n            raise SetupError(\n                f\"For broadband_method='pole_residue', 'num_freqs' must be >= 3, got {self.num_freqs}. \"\n                \"The vector fitting algorithm requires more frequency samples than fit coefficients.\"\n            )\n        return self\n\n    @cached_property\n    def frequency_grid(self) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"Frequency grid used to approximate frequency dependence.\n\n        For Chebyshev: returns ``num_freqs`` Chebyshev-spaced points.\n        For pole_residue: returns ``num_freqs`` uniformly spaced points.\n        \"\"\"\n        if self.num_freqs == 1:\n            return np.array([self.source_time._freq0])\n        freq_min, freq_max = self.source_time.frequency_range_sigma(sigma=CHEB_GRID_WIDTH)\n        if self.broadband_method == \"pole_residue\":\n            return np.linspace(freq_min, freq_max, self.num_freqs)\n        return self._chebyshev_freq_grid(freq_min, freq_max)\n\n    def _chebyshev_freq_grid(self, freq_min: float, freq_max: float) -> NDArray:\n        \"\"\"A Chebyshev grid based on a minimum and maximum frequency.\"\"\"\n        freq_avg = 0.5 * (freq_min + freq_max)\n        freq_diff = 0.5 * (freq_max - freq_min)\n        uni_points = (2 * np.arange(self.num_freqs) + 1) / (2 * self.num_freqs)\n        cheb_points = np.cos(np.pi * np.flip(uni_points))\n        return freq_avg + freq_diff * cheb_points\n\n\n\"\"\" Source current profiles determined by user-supplied data on a plane.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass CustomFieldSource(FieldSource, PlanarSource):\n    \"\"\"Implements a source corresponding to an input dataset containing ``E`` and ``H`` fields,\n    using the equivalence principle to define the actual injected currents.\n\n     Notes\n     -----\n\n        For the injection to work as expected (i.e. to reproduce the required ``E`` and ``H`` fields),\n        the field data must decay by the edges of the source plane, or the source plane must span the entire\n        simulation domain and the fields must match the simulation boundary conditions.\n\n        The equivalent source currents are fully defined by the field components tangential to the\n        source plane. TODO add image here\n\n        ..\n            TODO is this generic? Only the field components tangential to the custom source plane are needed and used\n            in the simulation. Due to the equivalence principle, these fully define the currents that need to be\n            injected. This is not to say that the normal components of the data (:math:`E_x`, :math:`H_x` in our example)\n            is lost or not injected. It is merely not needed as it can be uniquely obtained using the tangential components.\n\n        ..\n            TODO add example for this standalone\n            Source data can be imported from file just as shown here, after the data is imported as a numpy array using\n            standard numpy functions like loadtxt.\n\n        If the data is not coming from a ``tidy3d`` simulation, the normalization is likely going to be arbitrary and\n        the directionality of the source will likely not be perfect, even if both the ``E`` and ``H`` fields are\n        provided. This can be\n        computed in our eigenmode solver :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver` and implement the mode simulation in\n        FDTD.\n\n        Mode sources are normalized to inject exactly 1W of power at the central frequency.\n\n        The modal source allows you to do directional excitation. Illustrated\n        by the image below, the field is perfectly launched to the right of the source and there's zero field to the\n        left of the source. Now you can contrast the behavior of the modal source with that of a dipole source. If\n        you just put a dipole into the waveguide, well, you see quite a bit different in the field distribution.\n        First of all, the dipole source is not directional launching. It launches waves in both directions. The\n        second is that the polarization of the dipole is set to selectively excite a TE mode. But it takes some\n        propagation distance before the mode settles into a perfect TE mode profile. During this process,\n        there is radiation into the substrate.\n\n        .. image:: /_static/img/mode_vs_dipole_source.png\n\n        **Practical Advice**\n\n        Place mode sources in waveguide sections with a uniform cross-section. The mode profile is\n        computed assuming translational invariance (or constant bend radius) along the injection axis.\n        For bent waveguides, set ``bend_radius`` and ``bend_axis`` accordingly. Avoid placing mode\n        sources at tapers, junctions, or other locations where the cross-section is changing.\n\n        .. TODO improve links to other APIs functionality here.\n\n    Example\n    -------\n    >>> from tidy3d import GaussianPulse\n    >>> pulse = GaussianPulse(freq0=200e12, fwidth=20e12)\n    >>> mode_spec = ModeSpec(target_neff=2.)\n    >>> mode_source = ModeSource(\n    ...     size=(10,10,0),\n    ...     source_time=pulse,\n    ...     mode_spec=mode_spec,\n    ...     mode_index=1,\n    ...     direction='-')\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n\n    :class:`tidy3d.plugins.mode.ModeSolver`:\n        Interface for solving electromagnetic eigenmodes in a 2D plane with translational invariance in the third dimension.\n\n    **Notebooks:**\n        * `Waveguide Y junction <../../notebooks/YJunction.html>`_\n        * `90 degree optical hybrid <../../notebooks/90OpticalHybrid.html>`_\n\n    **Lectures:**\n        * `Prelude to Integrated Photonics Simulation: Mode Injection <https://www.flexcompute.com/fdtd101/Lecture-4-Prelude-to-Integrated-Photonics-Simulation-Mode-Injection/>`_\n    \"\"\"\n\n    mode_index: NonNegativeInt = Field(\n        0,\n        title=\"Mode Index\",\n        description=\"Index into the collection of modes returned by mode solver. \"\n        \" Specifies which mode to inject using this source. \"\n        \"If larger than ``mode_spec.num_modes``, \"\n        \"``num_modes`` in the solver will be set to ``mode_index + 1``.\",\n    )\n\n\n\"\"\" Angled Field Sources one can use. \"\"\"\n\n\nclass AbstractAngularSpec(Tidy3dBaseModel, ABC):\n    \"\"\"Abstract base for defining angular variability specifications for plane waves.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass FixedInPlaneKSpec(AbstractAngularSpec):\n    \"\"\"Plane wave is injected such that its in-plane wavevector is constant. inject a plane wave in a finite region.\n\n    Notes\n    -----\n\n        The TFSF source injects :math:`1 W` of power per :math:`\\\\mu m^2` of source area along the :attr:`injection_axis`.\n        Hence, the normalization for the incident field is :math:`|E_0|^2 = \\\\frac{2}{c\\\\epsilon_0}`, for any source size.\n        Note that in the case of angled incidence, the same power is injected along the source's :attr:`injection_axis`,\n        and not the propagation direction. This allows computing scattering and absorption cross-sections\n        without the need for additional normalization.\n\n        The TFSF source allows specifying a box region into which a plane wave is injected. Fields inside this region\n        can be interpreted as the superposition of the incident field and the scattered field due to any scatterers\n        present in the simulation domain. The fields at the edges of the TFSF box are modified at each time step such\n        that the incident field is cancelled out, so that all fields outside the TFSF box are scattered fields only.\n        This is useful in scenarios where one is interested in computing scattered fields only, for example when\n        computing scattered cross-sections of various objects.\n\n        It is important to note that when a non-uniform grid is used in the directions transverse to the\n        :attr:`injection_axis` of the TFSF source, the suppression of the incident field outside the TFSF box may not be as\n        close to zero as in the case of a uniform grid. Because of this, a warning may be issued when nonuniform grid\n        TFSF setup is detected. In some cases, however, the accuracy may be only weakly affected, and the warnings\n        can be ignored.\n\n    See Also\n    --------\n\n    **Notebooks**:\n        * `Defining a total-field scattered-field (TFSF) plane wave source <../../notebooks/TFSF.html>`_\n        * `Nanoparticle Scattering <../../notebooks/PlasmonicNanoparticle.html>`_: To force a uniform grid in the TFSF region and avoid the warnings, a mesh override structure can be used as illustrated here.\n    \"\"\"\n\n    num_freqs: int = Field(\n        1,\n        title=\"Number of Frequency Points\",\n        description=\"Number of points used to approximate the frequency dependence of the injected \"\n        \"field. Keep this task focused on packaging, docs, and planning metadata; full tagged models remain for `task-002` and `task-003`.\n81\t- Model ordered overlap explicitly through `Scene.structures_in_resolution_order()`, sorting by resolved priority and then insertion order so later structures still win ties during sequential materialization.\n82\t- Keep the initial container layer serialization-light: `to_payload()`, `to_json_text()`, and `write_json()` are enough for snapshots and handoff, while `task-005` can generalize the shared model base.\n83\t- Use a generic family-tagged component envelope in the IR so Phase 1 can package realistic simulations before every feature family has concrete typed IR classes; later tasks can specialize payloads without changing bundle shape.\n84\t- Bundle packaging is directory-based: `manifest.json` points at a hashed `simulation.json` entrypoint, avoiding self-referential manifest hashing while staying suitable for remote upload or local caching.\n85\t- Core validation is checklist-driven: implemented feature tags pass, deferred or rejected tags fail early with explicit errors, and known primitive geometry payloads validate only when enough fields are present so placeholder tagged dicts can survive until their concrete family tasks land.\n86\t- Shared model behavior should live in `autofdtd.core.models`; public API and IR classes should subclass it rather than duplicating serialization or copy helpers in subsystem-local base classes.\n87\t- Primitive geometry stays axis-aligned in Phase 1 public models; scene-compilation transforms are still explicit so later `Transformed` and grouped-geometry tasks can lower onto the same contract instead of rewriting primitive handling.\n88\t- Structure precedence is now inspectable with `Scene.resolve_structure_at_point()`, which mirrors materialization order by applying primitive containment checks in resolved-priority order.\n89\t- Keep `GeometryArray` as a public wrapper only; repeated placements lower into ordinary grouped and transformed instances so runtime/compiler code can treat arrays as pre-expanded ordered geometry.\n90\t- Phase 1 `PolySlab` scope is intentionally limited to constant-cross-section extrusions of simple polygons on principal axes; non-zero `dilation` or `sidewall_angle`, self-intersections, and curved or boolean polygon features must fail explicitly until later geometry tasks land.\n91\t- Keep the feature ledger conservative for clipping: `ClipOperation` remains a deferred family in `planning.py`, but geometry validation explicitly allows the implemented subset and rejects unsupported boolean ops with clear errors.\n92\t- Phase 1 transform wrappers are rigid only; free-form affine matrices and exact boolean meshing remain out of scope even though the public model now supports grouped and transformed composition.\n93\t- Keep the top-level simulation grid surface strict: `grid_spec` must be a `GridSpec`, `AutoGrid` requires `GridSpec.wavelength`, and `QuasiUniformGrid` remains an explicit deferred error.\n94\t- Phase 1 AutoGrid is deliberately narrow: derive a vacuum baseline from wavelength and domain size, discretize piecewise with a simple `max_scale` grading pass, and limit refinement inputs to `LayerRefinementSpec` body and bound hints rather than full geometry-driven meshing.\n95\t- Keep Phase 1 subpixel support narrow and explicit: dielectric interfaces may use `PolarizedAveraging` or `Staircasing`, while metal, PEC, PMC, and lossy-metal interfaces stay staircasing-only until anisotropic media and conformal policies land.\n96\t- Treat PEC and PMC as explicit constitutive clamp modes in coefficient compilation and runtime helpers instead of pretending they are extremely lossy ordinary media.\n97\t- Phase 1 `PoleResidue` keeps complex numbers JSON-safe as `(real, imag)` tuples in the public API and IR so serialization stays stable without inventing ad hoc string encoding.\n98\t- Phase 1 PoleResidue runtime support is electric-only and uses one complex polarization accumulator per pole; magnetic dispersion remains out of scope until later material families require it.\n99\t- Phase 1 `Sellmeier` support is intentionally passive-only and homogeneous-only: `B_i >= 0`, `C_i >= 0`, zero-`C_i` terms fold into `eps_inf`, and all timestep execution reuses the existing electric-only `PoleResidueMaterialCoefficients` path instead of creating a new auxiliary-state layout.\n100\t- Phase 1 `Lorentz` is passive-only (`delta_eps >= 0`, `damping >= 0`, `frequency^2 != damping^2`), `Drude` is limited to damped poles (`damping > 0`) so it can lower cleanly onto the current pole-residue path, and `Debye` is passive-only (`delta_eps >= 0`, `tau > 0`).\n101\t- The current exact-hold pole-residue recurrence path can overflow for sufficiently stiff poles relative to `dt`; material compilation now raises an explicit error instead of emitting unusable coefficients, which is especially relevant for very small-`tau` Debye fits.\n102\t- Phase 1 anisotropy stops at diagonal tensor media: `AnisotropicMedium` is implemented and IR-lowered, `FullyAnisotropicMedium` remains an explicit deferred error for runtime compilation, and `Medium2D` remains a deferred direct-simulation feature with offline conversion helpers only.\n103\t- Advanced material policy is explicit rather than silent: `LossyMetalMedium` and perturbation media are parseable defer buckets with manual fallback helpers, while sampled `Custom*` media are parsed or bucketed only to produce clear reject errors.\n104\t- Phase 1 boundary runtime support now covers `Periodic`, `BlochBoundary`, `PECBoundary`, `PMCBoundary`, and baseline `PML`; `StablePML`, `Absorber`, and ABC-family entries remain outside the runtime compiler until later boundary tasks land.\n105\t- Conductor boundaries are represented as reflection-sign transforms rather than special-casing them inside the future timestep loop: PEC uses odd tangential electric and odd normal magnetic parity, while PMC uses the opposite parity assignment.\n106\t- Keep Phase 1 PML deliberately narrow: use Tidy3D-shaped `num_layers + parameters + extrude_structures` public models, compile one profile per boundary face, and treat the first runnable backend as a staged damping layer with persistent face memory rather than a full split-field CPML implementation.\n107\t- Keep `StablePML` as a preset-driven extension of the baseline staged PML backend in Phase 1 rather than a separate field-splitting formulation; runtime differentiation is through compiled profile metadata and defaults, not a distinct kernel family.\n108\t- Keep `Absorber` practical and explicit: Phase 1 uses a conductivity-ramp absorbing subset with no auxiliary memory contribution and a PEC-like outer-wall reflection policy, trading fidelity for a clear stable fallback when baseline PML is unsuitable.\n109\t- Keep `ABCBoundary` practical and narrow: Phase 1 implements only the explicit-parameter first-order subset, and automatic medium inference plus mode-based ABC stay deferred until scene-material sampling and mode-solver tasks are available.\n110\t- Keep runtime convergence explicit and narrow: Phase 1 shutoff is the Tidy3D-style ratio of instantaneous integrated electric-field intensity to its historical maximum, checked on a configurable step interval; material-aware CFL relaxation and richer convergence heuristics remain deferred.\n111\t- Keep runtime logging separate from benchmark metrics: Phase 1 emits deterministic progress records at step 0, configurable progress intervals, and final stop, while every shutoff check still lands in convergence evidence even when progress logging is downsampled.\n112\t- Keep Phase 1 source-time scope narrow and explicit: implement `GaussianPulse` and `ContinuousWave` as standalone immutable models first, preserve Tidy3D-style `freq0`/`fwidth`/`offset` semantics plus `remove_dc_component` on Gaussian pulses, and defer broader source-time families to their own tasks instead of hiding them behind loose dict payloads.\n113\t- Phase 1 `BroadbandPulse` is a clearly delimited analytic subset: represent it as a Gaussian-modulated carrier derived from `(freq_range, minimum_amplitude)` rather than trying to reproduce Tidy3D's licensed extension internals, and keep `CustomSourceTime` as explicit sample interpolation with nearest-value clamping outside the provided range.\n114\t- Phase 1 `UniformCurrentSource` uses primal-cell placement metadata rather than hidden source snapping: zero-size axes interpolate between neighboring cell centers when enabled, finite extents either select center-in-bounds cells or overlap-fraction weights when `confine_to_bounds=True`, and `\"total\"` amplitude normalization divides by the local transverse extent implied by the source geometry and resolved grid.\n115\t\n116\t##
